note: Vol. II No. 8, and the single most valuable issue in this reading range for the reconstruction, because page 2 column 5 is a survey of Chicago's public houses written by a man complaining that they are not good enough. It names the Sauganash as newly refitted and the LAKE HOUSE as a new house then BUILDING in Kinzie's Addition, and says where a bigger one ought to go. Around it: the town-election caucus at the Exchange Coffee House, the close of the Circuit Court's May term, twelve vessels anchored off the bar at once, the town charter still missing, and an advertising page carrying four new Chicago houses — Magie & Wilkinson, John Holbrook, P. Pruyne & Co. and James Grant — three of them with placements.

claims.notes:
THREE BUILDING FACTS ABOUT CHICAGO IN ONE PARAGRAPH, THREE WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE.

1. THE SAUGANASH HAS JUST BEEN REFITTED — 'repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness and taste'. The building is old news; its CONDITION on 1 July 1835 is not, and this says it was freshly done up and not shabby. 'so far as it goes' is the editor's qualification and it means small, not poor.

2. THE LAKE HOUSE IS UNDER CONSTRUCTION IN KINZIE'S ADDITION AND IS NOT YET FINISHED OR NAMED. 'There is a new house building in Kinzie's addition [to be] named we understand, the "Lake House."' Both halves matter: it is a BUILDING SITE at the scene date, north of the main branch, and even its name is reported at second hand ('we understand'). Anything the reconstruction puts on that spot on 1 July 1835 should be a structure going up, not a hotel open for business. This is the only dated statement of the Lake House's state that this corpus has produced.

3. NO HOUSE IN CHICAGO IS BIG ENOUGH, and the editor says where the big one should be: 'about double the size of that latter, erected this side of the river about the centre of Lake Street or in that vicinity.' That is a PROPOSAL and not a building — nothing stood there — but it fixes the Lake House's scale by comparison (a house double it would be the town's largest) and it tells you where the commercial centre of gravity was felt to be: the middle of Lake Street, south of the river.

WITH THE OTHER CLAIMS IN THIS READING RANGE the town's public houses at the scene date are: the Sauganash (refitted, unplaced here), the Exchange Coffee House (corner of Lake and Franklin), the Eagle Coffee House or Trowbridge's (Dearborn Street vicinity), the Tremont House (Dearborn Street), the New-York House (Lake Street), and the Lake House (building, Kinzie's Addition). Six houses and not one of them, on the editor's account, adequate.

The column is clipped at the right edge line by line; every supply is bracketed and none of them invents a name, a size or a street.

claims.notes:
NEARLY TWO HUNDRED CAUSES ON A CHICAGO DOCKET IN MAY 1835, and only two criminal indictments in the lot — one for theft, one for horse stealing, neither of which convicted (hung jury; indictment quashed). That is a litigious, low-crime, property-disputing town, which is what a place in the middle of a land boom would be.

THE COURT SAT IN THIS TOWN and the term ran under two weeks against an expected five or six. Combined with Edward W. Casey's office 'adjoining that of the Clerk of the Circuit Court' (1835-05-27), it establishes that the court and its clerk had premises here — the building is not named in any of these eight issues and that is a gap worth stating.

Judge Breese is minted with the forename SIDNEY on the warrant of the same issue's list of state appointments ('Sidney B[reese]', page 2 column 6, line 1975) rather than out of general knowledge.

claims.notes:
TWELVE VESSELS AT ANCHOR OFF THE BAR AT ONCE, counted by the editor on the morning of Monday 8 June 1835, all believed loaded with merchandize from the lower lakes. It is the single best image in this reading range of what the water off Chicago looked like three weeks before the scene date, and the phrase 'anchored OFF our harbor' is the operative one: they are lying in the open lake, not inside. The harbor works were unfinished (1835-03-25: $32,800 just appropriated 'towards the completion of our harbor'), so twelve hulls standing off and lightering in is the picture, not twelve hulls at wharves.

The marine list in the same issue independently records fourteen arrivals dated 7 June, which is the same fleet counted from the custom-house end and corroborates the twelve.

claims.notes: THE ELECTION KEEPS BEING ADJOURNED BECAUSE NOBODY IN CHICAGO HAS THE LAW. Second of three printings of this grievance (1835-05-20, here, 1835-06-24), and this is the one that says the election was actually POSTPONED 'some how or other, from time to time'. So on 1 July 1835 the town's government is the OLD board of Trustees under the 1833 charter, still in office past the date they should have been replaced, with an enlarged charter passed in February that nobody in the town has read. That is the constitutional position behind the 1835-06-17 town meeting, which asks 'the present Trustees' to clean the streets and offers to give them powers they may be found not to have.

AN OFFICE INSIDE A SHOP — 'Office in the Store of Hubbard & Co.' — which is a different and tighter relation than 'next door' or 'over': the lawyer worked in a corner of the merchant's building. Three of the four lawyers placed in this reading range are lodged in somebody else's commercial building (Grant in Hubbard & Co's store, Moore in Kinzie's new building, Heacock in a second storey opposite the Exchange), which is a fact about how professional work was housed in this town: no purpose-built offices, only rooms in stores.

THE STREET IS CHAINED, NOT STATED. Magie & Wilkinson's notice in this same issue puts 'Hubbard & Co's. brick store' in LA SALLE STREET, which carries Grant there; the placement's own anchor is the store and the street rides on that one witness, so if the chained reading is wrong Grant moves with it. The New York, Buffalo and Detroit references are trade credit references and place nothing.

'HUBBARD & CO'S. BRICK STORE', IN LA SALLE STREET — the only building in these eight issues whose WALL MATERIAL the papers state, and it is stated in passing by a neighbour giving directions. A brick store on La Salle Street in June 1835, with brick quoted at $5-6 the thousand in the same paper's prices current. It anchors two other claims (James Grant's office is in that store) and it is the strongest single argument this corpus offers for putting a masonry building into an otherwise timber town.

AND A SECOND NEW BUILDING BESIDE IT: 'the New Store, in La Salle street, a few doors South of' the brick one. New enough that the advertisement calls it 'the New Store' as a proper name.

THE CONFLICT, RECORDED NOT RESOLVED. Five days later the same firm advertises 'ROOMS over the store of the subscribers, next door to Messrs. Harmon, Loomis & Co.' (1835-06-16, read in the 06-17 issue) — and Harmon, Loomis & Co. state their own store to be in SOUTH WATER STREET. So Magie & Wilkinson are a few doors south of a La Salle Street building and next door to a South Water Street one, five days apart. A corner lot at La Salle and South Water reconciles them without strain and so does a loose use of 'next door'; NEITHER IS ASSERTED. What is certain from both notices is that their store had a second storey with lettable rooms over it.

The stock list is quoted in the goods field rather than in the quote: sixty-odd lines of it run down the column and the claim cites the head and the signature.

THE TOWN'S DRUGGIST IS ALSO ITS SHIP CHANDLER AND ITS HARVEST-TOOL DEALER, and the combination is the finding. Fourteen separate advertisements over this issue and the next, all signed P. Pruyne & Co.: French quinine by the ounce from named Paris chemists, morphine, iodine, belladonna — and in the same column rigging, cordage, twenty-two bales of oakum, caulking tools, sail needles, palms, pitch and tar, and twelve dozen grass scythes with twenty-five dozen hay forks. A single Chicago house supplying the apothecary, the harvest and the shipyard in June 1835.

THE OAKUM AND CAULKING TOOLS ARE THE INTERESTING PART: somebody in Chicago was paying vessels' seams in the summer of 1835, and twenty-two bales is a quantity. Nothing in this corpus names a shipyard, and this is the closest thing to evidence of one.

UNPLACED IN EVERY PRINTING — no street, no anchor, in any of the fourteen advertisements. A house of this size and range with no stated address is exactly the gap the page images or a later issue might close.

J. Bates jr. advertises as auctioneer 'at the old stand' in every issue from 1835-05-20. So: an auctioneer with an old stand, and a NEW auction room on Dearborn Street by mid-June 1835, large enough to hold both a two-day land auction and a public fair.

THAT IS A BUILDING THE RECONSTRUCTION HAS NO EQUIVALENT FOR — a large clear-span commercial room on Dearborn Street, in use for something other than trade three weeks before the scene date. It is the only Chicago interior in these eight issues that is described by what it can hold.

What was sold in it was fifty town lots of MARSEILLES, sixty-five miles down the Illinois — Chicago as the auction market for canal-line town lots, which is the land boom seen from its selling end.

claims.normalized: To Rent, [T]HE handsome and convenient Dwelling House, lately erected by Mr. Rezigue, [on] Kinzie's addition. For terms, [etc. apply to E. K. HUBBARD.] June 3, 1835.
claims.notes:
A DWELLING HOUSE 'LATELY ERECTED' IN KINZIE'S ADDITION, TO LET AND STANDING EMPTY IN JUNE 1835 — the second dated new building north of the main branch in this reading range, beside the Lake House then going up. 'handsome and convenient' is an advertiser's word and carries no plan; 'lately erected' is the fact, and it dates the structure to the months immediately before the scene date.

WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT KINZIE'S ADDITION AT THE SCENE DATE. Three separate notices in these eight issues put new construction there — John H. Kinzie's finished store with three office rooms (1834), this dwelling, and the Lake House building — and one of the three is empty and advertised. The Addition in mid-1835 is being built up faster than it is being occupied, which is a different picture from the crowded south-side streets the same paper describes.

THE BUILDER'S NAME. 'Rezigue' is what all four printings set and it is left alone: it is not obviously an OCR error for anything, no other witness in the corpus carries it, and inventing a French Chicago name here would be exactly the kind of improvement this project forbids.
